## Choosing, under constraints, against a stated criterion

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
What optimization is
:::

> Optimization is the discipline of **choosing**, **under constraints**, against a **stated criterion**.

::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[]{.dot}

### If nothing is chosen

It is simulation. A model evaluated, not searched.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### If nothing constrains

The answer is trivial, and the model is wrong.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[]{.dot}

### If the criterion is unstated

There is no problem yet. "Improve the plant" is not a criterion.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
"Maximize weekly contribution margin, in USD per week" is a criterion. Notice that it carries a unit.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:08 – 00:11] · WHAT OPTIMIZATION IS**

**SAY —**

"One sentence, and it is worth memorizing. Optimization is the discipline of choosing, under constraints, against a stated criterion.

Three tests follow from it.

If nothing is being chosen, you do not have an optimization problem. You have a simulation: a model evaluated, not searched. Plenty of good engineering is simulation. It is not this course.

If nothing constrains the choice, the answer is trivial and the model is wrong. Make infinitely much of the profitable thing.

And if the criterion is not stated, you do not yet have a problem at all. 'Improve the plant' is not a criterion. 'Maximize weekly contribution margin in USD per week' is one, and notice that the difference between them is mostly a unit."

**DO —** Ask for one example from the room of something they do that is simulation rather than optimization. Take one answer, not four.
:::

"Four places you will meet this, and one of them is probably yours.

Design: what to build, and how big. Planning and scheduling: what to make next week, and in what order. Operation: where to sit the set points today. And data: fitting a kinetic model or a battery equivalent circuit is an optimization problem, even though nobody calls it one.

The mathematics is identical in all four. The only thing that changes is what the symbols mean."

## Five stages. Every week of this course.

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
The optimization workflow
:::

::: {.steps}
::: {.step .c-teal}
[1]{.n}[Verbal]{.h}[the problem in prose]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-amber}
[2]{.n}[Specification]{.h}[sets, data, decisions, units]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-teal}
[3]{.n}[Algebra]{.h}[objective and constraints]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-teal}
[4]{.n}[Code]{.h}[Pyomo, or a worksheet]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-plum}
[5]{.n}[Interpretation]{.h}[status, values, duals]{.d}
:::
:::

::: {.lede}
Each stage consumes the artifact of the one before it and produces one that is more formal and less ambiguous. They are not interchangeable and they are not optional.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
Skipping stage 2 and writing code straight from a paragraph is the commonest cause of a model that runs, returns a number, and is wrong.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:14 – 00:20] · THE FIVE-STAGE WORKFLOW**

**SAY —**

"This is the spine of the course. Five stages, and every week returns to them.

One, the verbal problem: what decision is being made, and by whom. Two, the structured specification: sets, data, decisions, one goal and numbered restrictions, every one of them carrying a unit. Three, the algebra. Four, the code. Five, the solution and what it actually means.

Each stage eats the artifact of the previous one and produces something more formal and less ambiguous. They are not interchangeable, and none of them is optional.

Now the sentence I want you to carry out of this room. Skipping stage two, and writing code straight from a paragraph of English, is the commonest cause of a model that runs, returns a number, and is wrong.

Almost every serious error in applied optimization can be located at one specific stage. Naming the stage is how you find the error."

**DO —**

- Point at the board where the five names are written and say they stay there for the whole hour.
- Every homework and every project deliverable in this course is one of these five artifacts. Say so.
:::

## What each stage produces, and how each one fails

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
The workflow, in a table
:::

| Stage | Artifact it produces | Characteristic failure |
|---|---|---|
| **1 Verbal** | Prose, plus a data source for every number in it | Optimizing the wrong thing, or a decision the plant cannot execute |
| **2 Specification** | Sets, parameters with units, variables with units, one objective, numbered restrictions | Missing constraint, unstated assumption, a parameter treated as a variable |
| **3 Algebra** | min *f*(*x*) subject to *g*(*x*) ≤ 0, *h*(*x*) = 0, every symbol defined | Units that do not balance, an index on one side only, accidental nonlinearity |
| **4 Code** | A Pyomo `ConcreteModel`, or a worksheet layout | Data typed into model logic, an off-by-one index, a sign error |
| **5 Interpretation** | Status, values, duals, a figure, one actionable sentence | Reporting numbers without reading the status |

::: {.foot}
::: {.flag}
Three rules: stage 2 before any algebra; every symbol carries a unit; no number is quoted until the termination condition has been read.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:20 – 00:23] · ARTIFACTS AND FAILURES**

**SAY —**

"Same five stages, with the artifact and the characteristic failure of each.

Read the right-hand column. Every one of those is a failure I have seen in a thesis, and none of them is a failure of arithmetic.

Three rules come out of this table, and I will hold you to all three. Stage two is written before any algebra. Every symbol carries a unit at the moment it is introduced. And no number is quoted until the termination condition has been read."

**DO —** Do not read the table aloud row by row. Give them fifteen seconds on the right-hand column, then move.
:::

## Stage 1 · a plant that makes two things

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
The verbal problem
:::

A unit supplying the zinc-air battery industry makes two products on shared equipment: an electrolyte **Additive** that suppresses zinc dendrite growth, and a **Binder** solution for air-cathode coating. Both pass through a reactor train, then separation and drying, then finishing and packaging. The plant plans one week at a time.

| Resource | Additive, h/t | Binder, h/t | Available, h/week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reactor train | 3 | 2 | 24 |
| Separation and drying | 1 | 2 | 16 |
| Finishing and packaging | 1 | 1 | 9 |
| **Contribution margin, USD/t** | **400** | **300** | |

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
The reactor train is shared with other campaigns, which is why only 24 h/week are allocated. Contribution margin is selling price minus variable cost. Everything produced can be sold. Choose the weekly plan with the largest total contribution margin.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:23 – 00:27] · STAGE 1, THE VERBAL PROBLEM**

**SAY —**

"One small problem, and we walk all five stages on it, so that you see the whole pipeline once before we break it into pieces.

A specialty unit supplying the zinc-air battery industry makes two things on shared equipment. An Additive that suppresses dendrite growth, and a Binder for the air cathode. Three shared resources: a reactor train, separation and drying, and finishing and packaging.

The table is the data. Three hours of reactor per tonne of Additive, two per tonne of Binder, twenty-four hours a week available because the reactor is shared with other campaigns. Margins of four hundred and three hundred US dollars a tonne.

That is all of stage one. Notice what it already contains: a unit on every number, and a reason for every limit."

**DO —**

- Say the last sentence of the footnote out loud: everything produced can be sold. It is an assumption, and in three slides they will see it written down as a numbered restriction so that it can be challenged.
- This is the same model that runs in the Week 1 notebook and in the solution workbook. If a slide and a file ever disagree, the file is authoritative.
:::

## Stage 2 · the structured specification {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Written before any algebra
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
| Object | Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| set | *p* ∈ *P* | product on the shared equipment | – |
| set | *r* ∈ *R* | shared resource | – |
| parameter | *c*<sub>*p*</sub> | contribution margin | USD/t |
| parameter | *a*<sub>*rp*</sub> | use of resource *r* per tonne of *p* | h/t |
| parameter | *b*<sub>*r*</sub> | hours of *r* available | h/week |
| decision | *x*<sub>*p*</sub> ≥ 0 | tonnes of *p* made | t/week |
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.spec}
[Objective, in words]{.eyebrow}

Maximize total weekly contribution margin, in USD per week.
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-amber}
**Restrictions, in words**

1. Hours used on each resource cannot exceed hours available.
2. Production cannot be negative.
3. Everything produced can be sold, so there is no demand limit.
:::
:::
:::
::::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
R3 is an assumption. Writing it down as a numbered restriction is exactly what makes it possible to challenge it later.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:27 – 00:31] · STAGE 2, THE SPECIFICATION**

**SAY —**

"Stage two. No algebra yet, and that is the point.

On the left, every object in the problem with a symbol, a meaning and a unit. Two index sets, three parameters, one decision. On the right, the goal in one sentence, and the restrictions numbered in plain English.

Look at restriction three. Everything produced can be sold. That is not a fact about the plant; it is an assumption I have made. Writing it down and giving it a number is what makes it possible for somebody to walk in next week and say, actually, we cannot sell more than five tonnes of Binder.

An assumption that is not written down cannot be challenged. It just quietly determines your answer."

**DO —** If the room is with you, ask which of the three restrictions is the one that could be wrong. Somebody will say R3. If nobody does, say it yourself and move on.
:::

## Stage 3 · the algebra, and the units check

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
The mathematics, and the thirty-second habit
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.spec}
[General form]{.eyebrow}

maximize &nbsp; Σ<sub>*p*</sub> *c*<sub>*p*</sub> *x*<sub>*p*</sub> &nbsp; over *x* ≥ 0

subject to &nbsp; Σ<sub>*p*</sub> *a*<sub>*rp*</sub> *x*<sub>*p*</sub> ≤ *b*<sub>*r*</sub> &nbsp; for every *r*
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[This week's data, written out]{.eyebrow}

max &nbsp; z = 400 x₁ + 300 x₂ &nbsp;&nbsp; [USD/week]

s.t. &nbsp; 3x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 24 &nbsp;&nbsp; reactor

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 16 &nbsp;&nbsp; separation

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x₁ + x₂ ≤ 9 &nbsp;&nbsp; packaging

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x₁ ≥ 0, x₂ ≥ 0
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-amber}
**The units check**

On every constraint, [h/t] · [t/week] = [h/week], which matches the right-hand side.

In the objective, [USD/t] · [t/week] = [USD/week].
:::
:::

::: {.punch}
A units check catches more modeling errors than any other single habit, and it costs thirty seconds.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**[00:31 – 00:35] · STAGE 3, THE ALGEBRA**

**SAY —**

"Stage three. Now the mathematics, and it writes itself, because stage two did the work.

The general form at the top. The same thing with this week's numbers underneath. Three constraints, two variables, non-negativity.

And then the reason stage three exists as a separate stage at all. The units check. On every constraint, hours per tonne times tonnes per week gives hours per week, which is what the right-hand side is. In the objective, dollars per tonne times tonnes per week gives dollars per week.

Thirty seconds. It catches more modeling errors than any other habit I know. Do it on every model you write this semester, including the ones you are sure about."

**DO —** Write the units cancellation on the board while you say it. Watching it cancel is worth more than seeing it printed.
:::

## Stage 4 · the same model in two dialects {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Code
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-sage}
[Spreadsheet · W01_product_mix]{.eyebrow}

`B5:C5` changing cells, tonnes per week

`B8:C8` margins, blue: given data

`B12:C14` the coefficient block

`D12:D14` `=SUMPRODUCT($B$5:$C$5,B12:C12)`

`F12:F14` right-hand sides, own column

`D9` objective cell, Set Objective, To: Max
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[Pyomo · W01_introduction_first_model]{.eyebrow}

`m.P = pyo.Set(...)`, `m.R = pyo.Set(...)`

`m.margin = pyo.Param(m.P, ...)`

`m.use = pyo.Param(m.R, m.P, ...)`

`m.avail = pyo.Param(m.R, ...)`

`m.x = pyo.Var(m.P, domain=NonNegativeReals)`

`m.resource = pyo.Constraint(m.R, rule=...)`

`m.profit = pyo.Objective(..., sense=maximize)`
:::
:::
:::
::::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
One named component per algebraic object. Never type a number inside a formula, in either dialect.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:35 – 00:39] · STAGE 4, CODE**

**SAY —**

"Stage four, in two dialects, because this course uses both.

On the left the worksheet. On the right Pyomo. Look at how they line up. A set of products is a row of column headers, or it is a `Set`. The margins are a row of blue cells, or they are a `Param`. The changing cells are green, or they are a `Var` with a domain. One spreadsheet row per resource is exactly one `Constraint` index.

They are the same object wearing different clothes.

And one rule that holds in both. One named component per algebraic object, and never, ever type a number inside a formula. Data lives in cells with a colour, or in a `Param`. The moment a four hundred appears inside a `SUMPRODUCT`, the model has stopped being maintainable."

**DO —** Blue for given data, green for changing cells. Say the convention out loud; it is used in every workbook in this course.
:::

## Stage 5 · the solution, and what it actually says

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Read the status first, then the numbers
:::

| Resource | Used, h | Available, h | Slack, h | Status | Shadow price, USD/h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reactor train | 24 | 24 | 0 | binding | 100 |
| Separation and drying | 12 | 16 | 4 | slack | 0 |
| Finishing and packaging | 9 | 9 | 0 | binding | 100 |

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-teal}
**The answer**

**x\* = (6, 3)** t/week,&nbsp; **z\* = 3,300.00** USD/week.

Make 6 t of Additive and 3 t of Binder. Two resources are fully used; separation has 4 h/week to spare.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-amber}
**The identity that is not a coincidence**

100(24) + 0(16) + 100(9) = 3,300, which is exactly z\*.

That is strong duality, and it is Week 8.
:::
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**[00:39 – 00:43] · STAGE 5, THE SOLUTION**

**SAY —**

"Stage five. And it begins with the status, not with the objective value. We come back to why in the next block.

The plan is six tonnes of Additive and three of Binder, worth three thousand three hundred dollars a week. Two of the three resources are fully used, the reactor and the packaging line. Separation and drying has four hours a week spare.

Now look at the last column. One extra reactor hour per week is worth a hundred dollars. One extra packaging hour is also worth a hundred. And one extra hour of separation is worth nothing at all, because separation is not what is stopping you.

And here is something that will look like a coincidence until Week 8. A hundred times twenty-four, plus zero times sixteen, plus a hundred times nine, is three thousand three hundred. Exactly the optimal value. That is the strong duality theorem, and it is not an accident."

**DO —** Numbers to have in your mouth: 24/24, 12/16, 9/9 hours; shadow prices 100, 0, 100 USD per hour. They recur in the summary and in Week 8.
:::

## Optimal, infeasible, unbounded {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Three outcomes, read in this order
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-sage}
[]{.dot}

### Optimal

A feasible solution exists and cannot be improved. Read the plan, then the constraint activity, then the duals, then write one sentence an engineer can act on.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[]{.dot}

### Infeasible

No plan satisfies every constraint at once. The feasible region is empty. This is a statement about the **model**.
:::

::: {.card .c-plum}
[]{.dot}

### Unbounded

The region is non-empty but the objective improves without limit. In a physical problem this always means a **constraint has been forgotten**.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
Read `solver.termination_condition`, not the coarse status. In Pyomo, assert it after every solve. In Excel, read the Solver Results dialog before you look at the sheet. Both broken models leave numbers on the screen if you do not check.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:43 – 00:47] · THREE OUTCOMES**

**SAY —**

"Three things a solver can tell you, and you read them in this order.

Optimal: a solution exists and cannot be improved. Then, and only then, you read the plan, the constraint activity, the duals, and you write one sentence somebody can act on.

Infeasible: nothing satisfies all the constraints at once.

Unbounded: the objective improves forever.

And here is the sentence I want you to remember. Infeasible and unbounded almost always mean the model is wrong, not that the problem is impossible. No real plant earns infinite margin, so unbounded is never news about the world.

One practical point. On a broken model the coarse status field often reads only error, which tells you nothing. The informative field is the termination condition, and it separates infeasible from unbounded. Assert it after every solve. In Excel, read the Solver Results dialog before you look at the sheet, because both of these leave numbers sitting on the worksheet."

**DO —** Write the Pyomo assertion on the board: `assert res.solver.termination_condition == pyo.TerminationCondition.optimal`. It appears in every notebook from here on.
:::

**[00:50 – 00:53] · THE AI POLICY**

**SAY —**

"Somebody is going to ask whether they may use ChatGPT for the homework, so I will answer it before it is asked, completely.

Yes. Generative AI is permitted for assignments and for the project, and drafting a model with it is expected rather than merely tolerated. Week six is a three-hour workshop on how to do exactly that.

What is graded is verification. You disclose which parts were AI-drafted and which tests validated them, and that disclosure is part of the report.

An unverified generated model earns no credit for model correctness. It can be beautifully formatted and confidently wrong, and it will score zero on that criterion.

And it is prohibited in both examinations. That is not ambiguous.

Notice that this is the same rule as the first slide of today. A solver answers the question you asked. So does a language model. The verification is your job either way, and in this course it is the part that carries the marks."

**DO —** Answer this directly and completely. It will be asked in the corridor otherwise, and the corridor answer travels further than the lecture one.
